cards.explanation: The answer is outside the camp. The person had been living out there alone (Leviticus 13:46), so the priest makes the trip to him. That's a priest who owns comfortable sandals, friends. He doesn't wait for anybody to show up at his door.

The answer is seven times. The text says, “Seven times he shall sprinkle the one to be cleansed of the skin disease.” Keep your eye on that number, because the oil gets sprinkled seven times later (Leviticus 14:16), and so does the house at the end (Leviticus 14:51). The priest isn't winging it with a flick and a shrug.

The answer is True. Right after the seven sprinklings, the text says, “Then he shall pronounce him clean…” (Leviticus 14:7). The priest is the one who says it out loud. That's a word the person has been waiting a long time to hear, I think.

The answer is that the live bird is released into the open field. The text says the priest “…shall pronounce him clean and release the live bird into the open field.” No altar for this one. It gets sent off into the open, and I think that bird has earned some sky.

The answer is outside his own tent. Leviticus 14:8 says, “…he may enter the camp, but he must remain outside his tent for seven days.” He's back in the camp, so that part's a win. But his own front door has to wait a week.

The answer is water. Leviticus 14:9 says, “He must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water, and he will be clean.” Water has already shown up in this passage, since the first bird was slaughtered over fresh water. Plain, simple, and it does the job.

The answer is at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, friends! Leviticus 14:11 says the priest presents the person with the offerings “…before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” Look at this guy: he's got two lambs, a ewe lamb, flour and oil, and he's standing right there in front of the LORD. I think that's a lot to carry, and I bet he's grinning anyway. Earlier in the passage he's outside the camp, and now here he is at the Tent of Meeting.

The answer is his right earlobe, his thumb and his big toe. Leviticus 14:14 says the blood goes on “…the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.” Ear, thumb, toe. Me, I'm a stamper with a mustache, so I've got no earlobes and no toes, just a mustache doing all the work.

The answer is to make atonement for him before the LORD. Leviticus 14:18 says the rest of the oil goes on his head “…to make atonement for him before the LORD.” I'm not adding any extra reasons to that. The text gives the purpose, so I'll stand right there with it.

The answer is altar. Leviticus 14:20 says the priest offers the burnt offering “…on the altar, with the grain offering, to make atonement for him, and he will be clean.” That's the end of the first long list of offerings. The eighth day is a full one.

The answer is lamb. Leviticus 14:21 says the poor person “…is to take one male lamb as a guilt offering…” Compare that with verse 10, where the other list has two male lambs and a ewe lamb. The poor person's list is shorter, but the guilt offering is still a lamb.

The answer is whichever he can afford. Leviticus 14:22 says, “…two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford…” The choice goes by what the person has. The text gives the poor person that room, and I like it.

The answer is False. The poor person still gets the blood on the right earlobe, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot (Leviticus 14:25). Then the oil goes “…on the same places as the blood of the guilt offering.” (Leviticus 14:28). The list of offerings is smaller, but the steps are the same.
The answer is to come and tell the priest. Leviticus 14:35 says, “…the owner of the house shall come and tell the priest…” The owner doesn't handle it alone. He brings it to the priest.

The answer is cleared, and it's smart. Leviticus 14:36 says, “The priest must order that the house be cleared before he enters it to examine the mildew…” Then comes the reason: “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” So everything comes out before the priest steps in. That's the kind of order I like, friends. Empty the house first, then look at the walls.

The answer is so nothing in it becomes unclean. Leviticus 14:36 gives the reason: “…so that nothing in the house will become unclean.” The text states the reason plainly, so I don't need to add one. The house gets cleared first, then the priest goes in.

The answer is that the stones are pulled out and thrown outside the city. Leviticus 14:40 says he “…must order that the contaminated stones be pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city.” The stones leave the house and the city. Imagine hauling that load, friends.

The answer is False. When the mildew reappears and spreads, Leviticus 14:44 says, “…it is a destructive mildew; the house is unclean.” Then the house “…must be torn down with its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster…” (Leviticus 14:45). No second replastering is offered.

The answer is True. Leviticus 14:46 says, “Anyone who enters the house during any of the days that it is closed up will be unclean until evening.” The seven days start when the priest closes it up (Leviticus 14:38). So that's a house to stay out of.

The answer is clothes. Leviticus 14:47 says, “And anyone who sleeps in the house or eats in it must wash his clothes.” Sleeping in it or eating in it, both count. The laundry bill on this one is real.
The answer is True. Leviticus 14:55 says this law covers “…mildew in clothing or in a house…” So clothing is named right alongside the house. The same law covers both.

The answer is to tell when something is clean or unclean. Leviticus 14:57 says the law is “…to determine when something is clean or unclean.” Skin, mildew, a rash or a spot, it's all under that same purpose. The text gives the reason, and I'm happy to leave it there.
